report:
**Conclusion: The claim as stated is false/misleading.** Food-grade fruit waxes themselves (carnauba, shellac, candelilla, beeswax, or petroleum-based food-grade waxes) are not carcinogenic. They are approved by the FDA as safe food additives and are simply replacing the natural wax that apples produce and that gets washed off during processing (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/you-asked/why-do-they-spray-wax-apples-0; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruit_waxing).

The nuance behind the myth involves **morpholine**, a chemical sometimes used as an emulsifier to help wax formulations adhere and spread on U.S. apples. Morpholine itself is not classified as a human carcinogen at the tiny residual levels found on fruit (typically millionths of a gram after evaporation during application), but concern exists because it can react with nitrites in the digestive tract to form N-nitrosomorpholine, a compound shown to be carcinogenic in animal studies (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/critical-thinking-health-and-nutrition/waxing-lyrical-about-fruit-wax; https://goodfruit.com/european-rule-takes-the-shine-off-apples/). This precautionary concern led the EU to ban morpholine-containing wax on imported apples starting around 2010–2011, even though the US, Canada, and other countries still permit it in small amounts under food-safety regulations.

So the evidence shows: (1) the waxes themselves are safe and FDA-approved; (2) morpholine, an additive in some wax formulations (not universal to all "food-grade wax"), is the actual point of scientific debate, and the concern is theoretical/precautionary based on nitrosamine formation rather than established direct causation of cancer in humans from eating waxed apples. The blanket claim "wax coatings cause cancer" overstates and misattributes the actual, narrower, unresolved concern about morpholine-based formulations.

**Recommendation:** If concerned, wash apples or choose ones without morpholine-based coatings; the wax itself is not the hazard.
